title: Arroz con pollo
skill: Rice cooked by absorption with the chicken

notes.1: Fills one large pot. The rice's ratio is worked out for this size, so cook two pots for more.

move.title: Toast it, measure it, leave it
move.body: Arroz con pollo, chicken with rice, is a one-pot dinner cooked all over Latin America; this is the Cuban way, golden and full of sofrito. The rice cooks by absorption: it takes in a measured amount of liquid and nothing is drained. Today you'll brown the chicken, build a sofrito, toast the rice in it, add exactly 1¾ cups of liquid for every cup of rice, and let the chicken finish cooking on top, under the lid.

why.title: Brown, don't cook through
why.body: Browning the chicken in a hot pot makes a golden crust and leaves browned bits on the bottom that flavor the rice. It doesn't need to be cooked through yet: it finishes in the steam on top of the rice.

why.title: The sofrito
why.body: Onion, green pepper, and garlic cooked slowly in oil until soft and sweet are the base of Cuban cooking. Their liquid loosens the browned bits from the chicken, so the flavor goes into the rice.

why.title: Toast the rice
why.body: Stirred in the hot oil for 2 minutes, each grain gets a coat of fat and turns a little see-through at the edges. Coated grains soak up liquid evenly and cook up separate instead of sticky.

why.title: 1¾ cups for each cup
why.body: Plain long-grain rice takes about 1½ cups of water for each cup. Here it takes about 1¾, because it cooks longer, under the chicken, in a thick sauce. The tomato sauce counts: 1 cup of it and 2½ cups of broth make the 3½ cups for 2 cups of rice. Too much, and it's mushy; too little, and it's crunchy.

why.title: Lid on, heat low
why.body: The water at the bottom boils; the steam rises and cooks the top layer and the chicken. Lifting the lid lets the steam out, and stirring breaks the grains and makes them gluey.

why.title: 165°F in the thickest piece
why.body: The chicken is safe when its thickest part reads 165°F. The pieces were cut the same size, so the biggest one tells you about all of them.

wrong.sign: The rice is crunchy on top
wrong.fix: Steam escaped, or it needed a few more minutes. Sprinkle ¼ cup of hot broth over the top, cover, and cook 5 more minutes on low.

wrong.sign: The rice is wet and mushy
wrong.fix: Too much liquid, or it was stirred. Leave the lid off on low heat for 5 minutes to dry it. Measure the liquid exactly next time.
The heat was too high under the lid. Don't scrape the scorched part into the rest; serve from the top. Use the smallest burner on low next time.

wrong.sign: The chicken didn't brown; it went pale and wet
wrong.fix: The pot wasn't hot enough or was crowded. Brown it in two batches, and pat it dry first.

quiz.q: How much liquid for each cup of rice in arroz con pollo?
quiz.explain: Plain rice takes 1½; the sauce and the chicken on top call for a little more, and the tomato sauce counts.

quiz.q: Why toast the rice in the sofrito?
choices: Fat-coated grains cook evenly and stay separate

quiz.q: Why don't you lift the lid while the rice cooks?
choices: The steam escapes and the top layer won't cook

quiz.q: Why does the chicken only brown at the start?
choices: It finishes cooking in the steam on top of the rice

steps.text: Cut the onion and the green pepper into ¼-inch dice. Mince the garlic. Keep them in separate piles on the board, then move them to a plate so the board is free for the chicken.
Put the rice in the colander and rinse it under cold water, swishing it with your hand, until the water running out is nearly clear. Leave it to drain.

Pat the chicken dry with paper towels. Trim off any thick pieces of fat with the chef's knife, and cut each thigh in half so the pieces are about the same size. Put them in the bowl. Squeeze in the lime's juice, add the chicken's cumin, oregano, salt, and pepper, and toss with the tongs.
steps.tip: The chicken sits in the lime while you wash up and get the pot hot.

steps.text: Wash the board and knife in hot, soapy water, throw away the paper towels, and wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lift the chicken out of the bowl with the tongs, letting the juice drip off, and brown half of it on both sides, 3 minutes a side. Move it to the plate, and brown the rest.
steps.look: Golden brown on both sides. It isn't cooked through yet.

steps.text: Wash the bowl and the tongs in hot, soapy water, and wash your hands with soap.
Turn the heat to medium. Add the last tablespoon of oil, then the onion and green pepper. Cook, stirring and scraping up the browned bits, until soft. Add the garlic and stir for 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft and glossy, with no browned bits left stuck to the pot.

steps.text: Add the drained rice, turmeric, and the rice's cumin. Stir for 2 minutes, until every grain is yellow and coated.
steps.look: Shiny grains, a little see-through at the edges.

steps.text: Measure the tomato sauce and the broth exactly and pour them in with the bay leaf and the rice's salt. Stir once, scraping the bottom, and bring it to a boil.
Nestle the chicken pieces into the top of the rice with their juices. Put the lid on, turn the heat to low, and don't lift the lid until the timer rings.

Lift the lid away from you. Push the thermometer into the thickest piece of chicken. It needs to read 165°F. Taste a few grains from the top: soft, with no hard center. If either isn't there, cover and cook 5 more minutes.
Scatter the peas over the top, put the lid back on, and turn off the heat. Let it rest.
steps.tip: The peas heat through in the steam.

steps.text: Take out the bay leaf. Fluff the rice around the chicken with the fork, and lay the red pepper strips and olives on top if you're using them.
